title: Harvey Raises Growth Round at $11 Billion Valuation, Co-led by GIC and Sequoia
author: Harvey Team

dom.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source supports Harvey as a prominent test case for specialised legal-AI durability, citing major financing and substantial company-reported adoption as evidence of investor and purchaser confidence. It also supports the view that stronger foundation models do not automatically eliminate the application layer because deploying them in complex legal workflows requires specialised judgment. However, it provides no independent evidence of productivity, accuracy or durable competitive advantage.
qs: On Wednesday, the legal AI company announced it's raised $200 million in fresh capital at a valuation of $11 billion.
Grady said that because model capabilities are improving so quickly, trying to apply them in real-world situations is a bigger undertaking than it has been for software companies in the past.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s market-traction and application-layer claims: it reports substantial funding and company-reported adoption while presenting specialised AI deployment as requiring meaningful judgment beyond frontier-model access. It does not independently establish accuracy, productivity, intensive use, or the cluster’s specific prestige-and-governance thesis.
qs: The company's products are used by more than 100,000 lawyers across 1,300 organizations, according to a release.
Grady said that because model capabilities are improving so quickly, trying to apply them in real-world situations is a bigger undertaking than it has been for software companies in the past.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source reinforces the synthesis’s distinction between strong commercial traction and proven defensibility. It reports rapid ARR growth, adoption and agent deployment, while attributing productivity and application-layer advantages to Harvey or its investor rather than treating them as independent evidence of durable leadership.

kp.k: Harvey claims agents increasingly execute complete legal workflows
kp.d: In its 25 March 2026 announcement, Harvey asserts that agents undertake high-volume and increasingly complex legal tasks from start to finish, freeing lawyers for higher-value work. It names Ashurst, Baker Donelson, Cuatrecasas and GSK Stockmann as firms deploying agents across their practices. This is the vendor’s account of task restructuring, rather than a reported study measuring productivity or workforce effects.
qs: AI agents are rapidly changing legal work as they take on high-volume, increasingly complex tasks and run workflows from start to finish, freeing up lawyers to focus on higher-value work.
Leading law firms including Ashurst, Baker Donelson, Cuatrecasas, and GSK Stockmann are among those deploying agents across their practices.

kp.k: Funding targets custom agents and embedded legal engineering
kp.d: Harvey says its $200M round will expand the more than 25,000 custom agents customers run on its platform and scale embedded legal engineering teams that build and optimize agents inside law firms and corporate legal departments. CNBC likewise reports planned worldwide expansion of those teams. The stated investment priorities couple agent deployment with implementation work inside customer organizations.
qs: The funding will be used to expand the more than 25,000 custom agents our customers run on Harvey and to scale the embedded legal engineering teams that help build and optimize those agents inside the world’s top law firms and legal departments.
The company will also grow its embedded legal engineering teams around the world.

kp.k: Reported adoption spans law firms and enterprise legal buyers
kp.d: CNBC reports that Harvey’s tools can streamline contract analysis, compliance, due diligence and litigation. Citing a release, it gives adoption figures of more than 100,000 lawyers across 1,300 organizations and identifies global law firms, NBCUniversal and HSBC among clients. These are reported usage and customer figures, not measured improvements in legal work.
qs: Founded in 2022, Harvey offers AI tools for legal and professional services that can streamline contract analysis, compliance, due diligence and litigation.
The company's products are used by more than 100,000 lawyers across 1,300 organizations, according to a release.
Clients include global law firms and large enterprises like NBCUniversal and HSBC.

kp.k: Revenue and financing figures indicate rapid commercial expansion
kp.d: CNBC reports annual recurring revenue of $190 million in January, up from the $100 million figure announced in August. The March 2026 financing raised $200 million at an $11 billion valuation, co-led by GIC and Sequoia. TechCrunch reports more than $1 billion in cumulative funding and a valuation increase of over 3.5x in a year, tracing valuations from $3 billion in February 2025 to $5 billion in June and $8 billion in December.
qs: The company hit $190 million in annual recurring revenue in January, up from the $100 million figure it announced in August.
Today we’re announcing that we’ve raised $200M at an $11 billion valuation.
The round is co-led by GIC and returning investor Sequoia.
With this new funding, the company has raised more than $1 billion in total, and its valuation jumped over 3.5x in a year.

Harvey was valued at $8 billion from a round announced in December, led by Andreessen Horowitz. Before that, it was valued at $5 billion from a round led by Kleiner Perkins and Coatue, announced in June, and was at $3 billion from a Sequoia-led raise announced in February 2025.

kp.k: CNBC frames Harvey as evidence for vertical AI traction
kp.d: CNBC presents Harvey as an example of industry-specific AI startups gaining traction despite concerns that OpenAI and Anthropic will capture most industry value as they expand their offerings. This is the outlet’s market interpretation of Harvey’s growth, not a finding that specialized legal vendors are insulated from foundation-model competition.
qs: Harvey is showing that AI startups focused on specific industries are able to get traction even as OpenAI and Anthropic continue expanding their offerings.

With OpenAI and Anthropic soaring to a combined valuation of more than $1 trillion, some in the artificial intelligence industry fear that the two big model companies are sucking up so much of the value that there won't be much left for other startups.

kp.k: Investor emphasizes judgment in translating models into applications
kp.d: Sequoia partner Pat Grady argues that rapid improvements in model capabilities make real-world application a larger undertaking than for earlier software businesses, requiring craft, taste and judgment. He compares Harvey’s AI-native application approach to Salesforce’s role in the cloud transition. These are an investor’s assessments and analogy, rather than independently demonstrated competitive advantages.
qs: Grady said that because model capabilities are improving so quickly, trying to apply them in real-world situations is a bigger undertaking than it has been for software companies in the past.
There's a lot of craft, taste and judgment that goes into determining how to use AI to achieve a particular job, he said.

"They sort of wrote the playbook for what it means to be an AI-native application company, which is the same thing Salesforce did back in the day with the cloud transition," Grady told CNBC in an interview.

kp.k: Weinberg predicts success depends on relentless organizational adaptation
kp.d: Harvey CEO Winston Weinberg cautions against complacency and predicts that successful companies will continually adapt because the process of building a company is changing. His remarks concern company strategy in the AI market, rather than a specific prediction about law-firm staffing, pricing or lawyer displacement.
qs: "I think any company right now, the worst mistake you can possibly do is become complacent, because how you build a company is completely changing," Weinberg said in an interview.
"The companies that succeed are going to be the ones that are relentlessly adapting."

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Harvey Team claims agents already perform increasingly complex legal workflows, shifting lawyers toward higher-value work.
pts.d: The company describes agents taking on high-volume tasks and running workflows from start to finish. CNBC separately describes Harvey's tools as capable of streamlining contract analysis, compliance, due diligence and litigation. These are workflow-automation and augmentation claims; neither passage specifies that legal outputs may be relied on without human verification or predicts lawyer job losses.

pts.k: Harvey Team announces further expansion of custom agents and embedded legal engineering teams.
pts.d: The company states that its new funding will expand customers' use of custom agents and the teams that build and optimize them within law firms and corporate legal departments. CNBC attributes the same intended uses of capital to CEO Winston Weinberg. This is an announced investment plan, not a demonstrated future productivity outcome.

pts.k: CNBC presents Harvey as evidence that industry-specific AI vendors can gain traction despite expansion by foundation-model companies.
pts.d: CNBC frames Harvey's adoption, revenue growth and financing as a counterpoint to concerns that OpenAI and Anthropic will capture most AI-market value. Sequoia investor Pat Grady characterizes Harvey as a model for AI-native application companies. TechCrunch author Julie Bort similarly characterizes Harvey as a major AI-era commercial success and documents its financing trajectory. These claims concern a legal-tech vendor's commercial position, not the market share or profitability of law firms or ALSPs.

pts.k: Pat Grady claims rapidly improving models make real-world implementation unusually demanding; Winston Weinberg predicts that successful companies will adapt continuously.
pts.d: Grady's claim concerns the work of translating model capability into useful applications, emphasizing craft and judgment rather than automatic realization of benefits. Weinberg offers a broader business prediction about adaptation as company-building changes. These are attributed judgments about AI application businesses, not measured findings about legal practitioners' performance.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The workflow claims are supported by company-reported deployment counts and named adopters, rather than task-performance measurements.
pts.d: Harvey Team names four firms deploying agents and reports more than 25,000 custom agents in customer use. CNBC cites a release for use by more than 100,000 lawyers across 1,300 organizations and names enterprise clients. These provide adoption evidence; the document supplies no benchmarks, quantified time savings, quality measurements or detailed case studies demonstrating complexity handled or higher-value work enabled.

pts.k: Commercial-traction claims draw on financing and revenue figures; implementation and adaptation claims draw on investor and executive judgment.
pts.d: The reported $200 million financing at an $11 billion valuation, revenue growth and repeated investor participation support the articles' commercial-growth framing. TechCrunch traces valuation growth from $3 billion in February 2025 to $11 billion in March 2026. Grady is a partner at an investing firm and Weinberg is Harvey's CEO; their implementation and adaptation statements are offered as interview judgments, without comparative studies or tests of the predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Workflow change and commercial adoption are presented as current in March 2026; expansion and adaptation claims are forward-looking without a fixed deadline.
pts.d: All three pieces are dated 25 March 2026. Harvey describes agents as already changing work and being deployed. Funding-supported expansion is prospective, with no completion date or projected adoption target. CNBC's January and August revenue references imply January 2026 and August 2025 in context. Grady links implementation demands to rapidly improving model capabilities; Weinberg makes relentless adaptation a condition of future company success without specifying a forecast horizon.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified beneficiaries and participants are lawyers, major law firms, corporate legal departments, embedded legal engineers and specialized AI vendors.
pts.d: Lawyers are described as gaining capacity for higher-value work as agents handle workflows. Named law firms deploy agents across practices, while corporate legal departments and enterprise clients also use Harvey's products. Embedded legal engineering teams are to expand to support implementation. The market argument concerns specialized AI vendors and their investors amid foundation-model-provider expansion. The document does not specify effects on junior hiring, firm staffing structures, client fees or access to justice.
